content: Take appropriate corrective steps to optimize ventilation. Continue ventilating at a rate of 40 breaths per minute. Consider increasing the oxygen concentration if necessary. Perform suctioning if required. If the heart rate (HR) is less than 100 beats per minute, initiate chest compressions until the HR reaches 100 beats per minute or higher. Administer higher oxygen concentrations as needed. If the HR remains below 60 beats per minute, consider additional ventilatory support or administer intravenous adrenaline. If the HR exceeds 100 beats per minute, continue monitoring and supportive care. The 2013 edition of the Pocket Book is designed for use by healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, and other health workers, who provide care for young children in first-level referral hospitals. This second edition is based on evidence from updated and published clinical guidelines by the World Health Organization (WHO). It is intended for both inpatient and outpatient care in small hospitals equipped with basic laboratory facilities and essential medicines. In some settings, these guidelines can also be applied in any facility where sick children are admitted for inpatient care. The Pocket Book is part of a series of tools supporting the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI). The guidelines require hospitals to have the capacity to perform essential investigations, such as pulse oximetry, blood glucose testing, blood smear examinations for malaria parasites, hemoglobin estimation, packed cell volume and full blood count, blood grouping and cross-matching, and basic microscopy of cerebrospinal fluid and urine. Where possible, facilities should also provide blood and urine cultures, ultrasound, and basic X-rays. Additionally, essential medicines for managing critically ill children must be available. These guidelines do not cover advanced or high-care treatment options, such as intensive care or mechanical ventilation. Instead, they focus on managing the leading causes of childhood mortality in developing countries, including neonatal conditions, pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria, meningitis, septicemia, measles and related complications, severe acute malnutrition, and pediatric HIV/AIDS. They also address some common surgical conditions that can be managed in small hospitals. Details of the evidence supporting the Pocket Book can be found on the WHO website, referencing the published guidelines listed in the bibliography. These guidelines are applicable in most regions worldwide and can be adapted to suit specific country circumstances. The online version will be updated regularly as new evidence becomes available.
